items.stem:
Beyond the eastern gate, beside two collapsed arches, stands a stone tower that once marked the beginning of a covered channel. Among the surviving records are a set of measurements made during later repairs, along with sketches of the workers' tools. These records show that maintenance required both specialized knowledge and regular labor. Some channels still guide rainwater into underground cisterns, although modern roads have altered the original drainage patterns. Modern surveys are helping researchers map the parts of the system that remain beneath the city's streets.

items.stimulus: At Petra, the Nabataean capital in present-day Jordan, reliable water supplies supported a population that grew around the city's markets and temples. The city's prosperity depended on channels, cisterns, and clay pipes that collected water from seasonal streams. The network of channels that carried water from the hills to the city <u>was built</u> and repaired over several centuries. Because flash floods could destroy sections of the system, Nabataean engineers reinforced vulnerable channels with stone and plaster. Archaeologists have used these remains to study how the city adapted its water system to an arid climate.
